This page is a reference. Every construct org2html knows how to parse appears
on it at least once, rendered by the same build that renders every other post
on {{{sitename}}}. Find the family you need, read the short note above it, and
look at the result.

Nothing here was dressed by hand. Each section names the syntax that produced
what you see, so the page doubles as a map of the source.

* Headings

The title at the top of this page is its only =<h1>=. Org's first level becomes
=<h2>=, and each level after it steps down one, so the page keeps a single
unbroken outline. The contents box at the top lists the first two levels,
because this page sets =toc:2=.

** A second-level heading
Rendered as =<h3>=.

*** A third-level heading
Rendered as =<h4>=.

**** A fourth-level heading
Rendered as =<h5>=.

***** A fifth-level heading
Rendered as =<h6>=, which is where HTML runs out of headings.

****** A sixth-level heading
Also =<h6>=. With the title holding =<h1>=, Org's fifth and sixth levels land
on the same element. Their classes still differ, =outline-5= against
=outline-6=, so a stylesheet can tell them apart.

******* A seventh-level heading
Past the sixth level there is no heading element left, so a deeper headline
becomes a list item that carries its own body, and it never joins the table of
contents.

** Task states, priorities and tags

This page defines its own task sequence with
=#+TODO: TODO NEXT WAITING | DONE CANCELLED=. States before the bar are open,
states after it are closed, and a closed state wears a class of its own.
Priorities can be a letter or a digit; Org hides them unless =#+OPTIONS= says
=pri:t=. A statistics cookie counts child tasks (=[1/3]=) or checkboxes
(=[50%]=), and a tag may carry =@= or =#=.

A headline fifteen stars deep is an inline task: a boxed note inside the
running text rather than the start of a new section. An =END= line closes it.

*************** TODO [#B] Check the tag chips on a narrow screen      :mobile:
*************** END

*** NEXT [#A] Ship this reference post [1/3]            :alpha:@work:#urgent:
**** DONE Pick the slug and the date
**** WAITING [#1] Review the Spanish twin [50%]
- [X] Headings through tables
- [ ] Code through includes
**** TODO Replace the placeholder cover

** Headings that stay out of the page

Three markers keep a subtree in the source and out of the output. The word
=COMMENT= right after the stars drops a headline and everything under it. A
=:noexport:= tag does the same when the page is built. An =:archive:= tag keeps
the headline, so the outline still shows the subtree exists, and drops what it
holds. The first two kinds sit directly below this paragraph, and you cannot see
either of them. The third comes next.

*** COMMENT Drafting notes for the second pass
Tighten the heading ladder before the Spanish twin is written.

*** Build log from the first draft                                :noexport:
Seventeen warnings, every one of them about a stray macro, all fixed.

*** An archived subtree                                            :archive:
This sentence lives in the source file and nowhere else.

** renderEveryConstructTheEngineKnowsWithoutAnyClientJavaScript

The headline above is a single sixty-character word with nowhere to break,
the kind a long function name produces. It is here so that a layout bug of that
kind shows up on this page before it shows up anywhere else.

* Planning and clocks

Org keeps scheduling on the line right under a headline, and time tracking in
=CLOCK:= lines and drawers. Its own exporter leaves all of that out by default;
this page opts in with =p:t= and =c:t=.

** NEXT Publish the Spanish twin
SCHEDULED: <2026-08-17 Mon 09:00 +1w> DEADLINE: <2026-08-21 Fri ++1m -3d>

That is a planning line with repeaters (=+1w= and =++1m=) and a warning period
(=-3d=). Each timestamp keeps the text you typed and gains a machine-readable
=datetime= attribute.

** DONE Draft this page
CLOSED: [2026-08-13 Thu 17:40]
CLOCK: [2026-08-13 Thu 14:05]--[2026-08-13 Thu 17:40] =>  3:35
:LOGBOOK:
CLOCK: [2026-08-12 Wed 09:10]--[2026-08-12 Wed 11:25] =>  2:15
CLOCK: [2026-08-11 Tue 16:00]--[2026-08-11 Tue 16:50] =>  0:50
:END:
:NOTES:
A drawer holds whatever Org should keep out of the way. This one is a custom
NOTES drawer, so it renders as a plain framed block.
:END:

A closed task carries a =CLOSED:= stamp. The =CLOCK:= line under it renders as
a measurement, with its start, its end and its duration each in an element of
their own. Older entries folded into a =:LOGBOOK:= drawer become an accordion
you can open.

** CANCELLED Ship a second default stylesheet
CLOSED: [2026-08-10 Mon 12:00]

* Paragraph furniture

Lines that start with a colon and a space are fixed-width text, kept exactly as
typed:

: $ org2html build content -o dist/blog --include-root includes
: ✓ content/engineering/everything-org2html-renders.en.org

Five or more dashes on a line of their own draw a rule, and
=#+ATTR_HTML: :class= picks one of three variants: dashed, tick and boxed-x.

-----

#+ATTR_HTML: :class org-hr--dashed
-----

#+ATTR_HTML: :class org-hr--tick
-----

#+ATTR_HTML: :class org-hr--boxed-x
-----

Two backslashes end a line without ending the paragraph,\\
so this sentence starts on a new line,\\
and so does this one.

With =-:t=, Org's default, three hyphens make an em dash --- like this ---
while two make an en dash for a range such as 2020--2026, and three dots make an
ellipsis... With =':t=, "straight quotes" and 'single ones' curl, and so does
the apostrophe in it's. A =\-= marks a soft hyphen, so a long word such as
extra\-ordinarily\-long\-winded breaks where you allowed it and nowhere else.

* Lists

A dash, a plus sign and an indented asterisk all start unordered items, and
indentation nests them:

- A dash starts an item
+ So does a plus sign
  * An indented asterisk nests one level down
    - And a deeper item nests a third level

Ordered items take a number and a period:

1. First, with a period
2. Second, with a period

Or a number and a parenthesis:

1) First, with a parenthesis
2) Second, with a parenthesis

A single blank line between items keeps them in one loose list, and a line
indented under an item continues it:

- The first loose item

- The second loose item, whose text runs long enough that
  the source wraps it onto a second line

- The third loose item

A =[@5]= cookie restarts the count wherever you need it:

1. [@5] Fifth, because the cookie says so
2. Sixth, counted on from there

Description lists pair a term with its definition, and a definition may run
over several lines:

- Term :: A definition on one line.
- A longer term :: A definition that keeps going past the first line of the
  source, because the continuation is indented under its item.

Checkboxes come in three states, and they nest:

- [-] Publish the reference post
  - [X] Write the English page
  - [ ] Write the Spanish twin
- [X] Build it with the local engine
- [ ] Replace the placeholder cover

* Tables

A rule under the first row makes that row a header. A row of =<l>=, =<c>= and
=<r10>= cookies sets each column's alignment and never renders. A row that
starts with =/= groups columns and never renders either. A =#+TBLFM:= line
under a table is Org's spreadsheet formula, and it renders nothing at all.
=#+CAPTION= and =#+NAME= ride on the table, so [[tbl-heading-levels][the next
table]] can be linked by name.

#+CAPTION: Where each Org headline level lands on this page.
#+NAME: tbl-heading-levels
| Org level | Element | Class hook |
|-----------+---------+------------|
| <l>       |   <c>   |      <r10> |
| /         |    <    |          > |
| 1         |   h2    |  outline-1 |
| 2         |   h3    |  outline-2 |
| 3         |   h4    |  outline-3 |
| 4         |   h5    |  outline-4 |
| 5         |   h6    |  outline-5 |
| 6         |   h6    |  outline-6 |
#+TBLFM: $3='(concat "outline-" $1)

Alignment can also ride on the rule itself: a colon at the left end, the right
end or both ends of a segment sets that column.

| Marker on the rule | Aligns | Class        |
|:-------------------+:------:+-------------:|
| =:---=             | left   | =org-left=   |
| =:---:=            | centre | =org-center= |
| =---:=             | right  | =org-right=  |

Org also reads the grid tables of table.el, drawn with =+= at every corner:

+----------------+--------------------------+
| Grid table     | Drawn with table.el      |
+----------------+--------------------------+
| Border rows    | dashes, with =+= corners |
| Rendered as    | an ordinary table        |
+----------------+--------------------------+

=#+ATTR_O2H= can point at the row, the column or the single cell that carries
the argument. The mark is structure, a class in the markup, so any stylesheet
can decide how it looks. This table highlights its own second row, its fourth
column and one cell:

#+CAPTION: Three ways to point at part of a table.
#+ATTR_O2H: :highlight-row 2 :highlight-col 4 :highlight-cell 2.1
| Keyword           | Marks                        | Example               | Class                 |
|-------------------+------------------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------|
| =:highlight-row=  | one body row, counted from 1 | =:highlight-row 2=    | =org-row--highlight=  |
| =:highlight-col=  | one column, header included  | =:highlight-col 4=    | =org-cell--highlight= |
| =:highlight-cell= | one cell, as column.row      | =:highlight-cell 2.1= | =org-cell--highlight= |

A table ten columns wide with one sixty-character word in it cannot fit the
reading column. Rather than crush the columns, the engine puts every table in a
frame that scrolls sideways. =org-wide= lets this one break out of the column
first:

#+CAPTION: The export switches this page sets, against Org's defaults and the engine's.
#+ATTR_HTML: :class org-wide
| Settings      | =toc= | =num= | =pri= | =p=   | =c=   | =^=  | =-= | ='=   | In one word                                                  |
|---------------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+------+-----+-------+--------------------------------------------------------------|
| Emacs default | =t=   | =t=   | =nil= | =nil= | =nil= | =t=  | =t= | =nil= | traditional                                                  |
| org2html      | off   | off   | =nil= | =nil= | =nil= | ={}= | =t= | =nil= | cautious                                                     |
| This page     | =2=   | =nil= | =t=   | =t=   | =t=   | ={}= | =t= | =t=   | renderEveryConstructTheEngineKnowsWithoutAnyClientJavaScript |

=org-full-bleed= runs a table to both edges of the window:

#+CAPTION: What the engine writes beside every page it builds.
#+ATTR_HTML: :class org-full-bleed
| File                   | What it is                           | Who reads it          |
|------------------------+--------------------------------------+-----------------------|
| =index.html=           | the page itself                      | the browser           |
| =index.vue=            | the same page as a Vue component     | a Vue host            |
| =metadata.json=        | the document's keywords and counts   | the site's indexes    |
| =og-metadata.json=     | the social card fields               | the page head         |
| =relations.json=       | breadcrumb, series and related posts | the site's navigation |
| =structured-data.json= | the JSON-LD graph                    | search engines        |

=#+ATTR_O2H: :chart bar= draws a table as a bar chart while the site builds. The
drawing is a picture of the table, and the table travels inside the figure so a
screen reader and a crawler still get the numbers. Six bars leave each label
about eight characters at full size, and these run to twenty-seven, so the chart
sets every label a step smaller and wraps it onto up to three lines under its
bar, breaking only between words.

#+CAPTION: The longest unbroken runs on this page, in characters.
#+ATTR_O2H: :chart bar :chart-axis characters :chart-label-col 1 :chart-value-col 3 :highlight-row 6
| Stress test                 | Section  | Characters |
|-----------------------------+----------+------------|
| Unbreakable heading word    | Headings |         60 |
| Single-token table cell     | Tables   |         60 |
| Inline code and verbatim    | Inline   |         70 |
| Bare URL in running text    | Inline   |        120 |
| Longest line of the verse   | Blocks   |        200 |
| Longest line of source code | Code     |        220 |

* Code

A source block names its language after =#+BEGIN_SRC=, and the build highlights
it with the grammar an editor would use. Every block gets a header bar with its
language, a copy button and line numbers. A line wider than the block scrolls
rather than wraps:

#+BEGIN_SRC javascript
// Fourteen of the class hooks on this page, on one line exactly 220 characters wide:
const pageHooks = ["org-inlinetask", "org-planning", "org-clock", "org-callout--danger", "org-tabs", "org-diagram", "org-embed--x", "org-hero", "org-low-level", "org-chart", "org-diff", "org-results", "org-dl", "org-ol"]
#+END_SRC

=:tangle src/lexer.ts= names the file a block belongs to, so the header shows
=lexer.ts=. This block is sixty lines long:

#+BEGIN_SRC typescript :tangle src/lexer.ts
// A deliberately small Org lexer. The real one also handles blocks, drawers
// and planning lines; this one only has to be long enough to scroll.
export type TokenType = "HEADING" | "LIST_ITEM" | "TABLE_ROW" | "KEYWORD" | "BLANK" | "TEXT"

export interface Token {
  type: TokenType
  value: string
  line: number
  level?: number
}

// One pattern per construct, tried in the order the loop below tests them.
const HEADING = /^(\*+)\s+(.*)$/
const LIST_ITEM = /^\s*(?:[-+*]|\d+[.)])\s+(.*)$/
const TABLE_ROW = /^\s*\|/
const KEYWORD = /^#\+(\w+):\s*(.*)$/

export function tokenize(source: string): Token[] {
  const tokens: Token[] = []
  const lines = source.replace(/\r\n?/g, "\n").split("\n")

  lines.forEach((raw, line) => {
    const trimmed = raw.trim()
    if (trimmed === "") {
      tokens.push({ type: "BLANK", value: "", line })
      return
    }

    // A headline only counts at column zero; an indented star is a bullet.
    const heading = raw.match(HEADING) (ref:heading)
    if (heading) {
      tokens.push({ type: "HEADING", value: heading[2], line, level: heading[1].length })
      return
    }

    const keyword = trimmed.match(KEYWORD)
    if (keyword) {
      tokens.push({ type: "KEYWORD", value: keyword[2], line })
      return
    }

    if (TABLE_ROW.test(raw)) {
      tokens.push({ type: "TABLE_ROW", value: trimmed, line })
      return
    }

    const item = raw.match(LIST_ITEM)
    tokens.push(
      item
        ? { type: "LIST_ITEM", value: item[1], line }
        : { type: "TEXT", value: raw, line },
    )
  })

  return tokens
}

// The outline is every headline, in document order.
export const outline = (tokens: Token[]): Token[] =>
  tokens.filter((token) => token.type === "HEADING")
#+END_SRC

The headline test sits on [[(heading)]]. That reference is a coderef: the source
marks the line with =(ref:heading)= at its end, the label disappears from the
block, and =[[(heading)]]= in the prose names the line it marked.

A named block and its =#+RESULTS:= travel together. The result is styled as
output rather than as one more example:

#+NAME: answer
#+BEGIN_SRC python :results output
print(6 * 7)
#+END_SRC

#+RESULTS: answer
#+BEGIN_EXAMPLE
42
#+END_EXAMPLE

Rust, a diff and Emacs Lisp. A =diff= block tints its added and removed lines
and drops the line numbers, since the diff carries its own gutter. There is no
Emacs Lisp grammar in the highlighter, so that block ships as plain text and
says so in its markup rather than pretending:

#+BEGIN_SRC rust
fn main() {
    let constructs = ["heading", "table", "math"];
    println!("{} constructs, one page", constructs.len());
}
#+END_SRC

#+BEGIN_SRC diff
--- a/everything-org2html-renders.en.org
+++ b/everything-org2html-renders.en.org
@@ -17 +17 @@
-#+OPTIONS: toc:t
+#+OPTIONS: toc:2 num:nil pri:t p:t c:t ^:{} -:t ':t
#+END_SRC

#+BEGIN_SRC emacs-lisp
(setq org-export-with-smart-quotes t
      org-export-with-planning t)
#+END_SRC

Code can also sit inside a sentence: src_python{sum(range(10))} is inline
source. This engine never runs code, so an inline Babel call placed here
call_answer() adds nothing to the page.

* Blocks

A quote block:

#+BEGIN_QUOTE
A document is a record of decisions. The *renderer* only has to keep them.
#+END_QUOTE

=#+ATTR_HTML: :class org-quote--pull= turns a quote into a pull quote:

#+ATTR_HTML: :class org-quote--pull
#+BEGIN_QUOTE
Decide in the build, and ship the reader a document rather than a program.
#+END_QUOTE

An example block keeps everything literally, markup and spacing included:

#+BEGIN_EXAMPLE
An example block is verbatim: *stars*, /slashes/ and ~tildes~ stay as typed,
    and so does    the spacing.
#+END_EXAMPLE

A verse block keeps its line breaks and its leading indentation:

#+BEGIN_VERSE
Sanitize by default,
  decide in the build,
    and ship the reader a document, not a program.
A verse keeps its line breaks and its indentation, so a line this long stays one line in the source and wraps only where the page runs out of room, and never where a parser decided to join it for you.
#+END_VERSE

#+BEGIN_CENTER
A centre block, for the rare line that earns it.
#+END_CENTER

Seven admonitions share four intents. =IMPORTANT= renders as a tip, =CAUTION=
as a warning and =ABSTRACT= as a note, each keeping its own name on the label:

#+BEGIN_NOTE
A note adds context the reader can skip.
#+END_NOTE

#+BEGIN_TIP
A tip suggests a better way to do something.
#+END_TIP

#+BEGIN_WARNING
A warning flags something that can go wrong.
#+END_WARNING

#+BEGIN_DANGER
Danger is for the one mistake you cannot undo, such as building with =--no-sanitize=.
#+END_DANGER

#+BEGIN_IMPORTANT
Important renders with the tip's colours and keeps its own label.
#+END_IMPORTANT

#+BEGIN_CAUTION
Caution renders with the warning's colours and keeps its own label.
#+END_CAUTION

#+BEGIN_ABSTRACT
Abstract renders with the note's colours and keeps its own label.
#+END_ABSTRACT

A block name the engine does not know becomes a =<div>= with a class of the
same name, so =#+BEGIN_ASIDE= is styled by whatever a stylesheet says about
=.org-aside=:

#+BEGIN_ASIDE
An aside: a generic special block, carrying its name as its class.
#+END_ASIDE

A =COMMENT= block sits between this paragraph and the next one. Nothing inside
it reaches the page.

#+BEGIN_COMMENT
Reviewer: check every callout against the Spanish twin before merging.
#+END_COMMENT

A =#+BEGIN_JSONLD= block is not content at all. It joins the page's structured
data, so it describes this page to a search engine without a reader ever
scrolling past it. One sits right here.

#+BEGIN_JSONLD
{
  "about": {
    "@type": "SoftwareSourceCode",
    "name": "org2html",
    "codeRepository": "https://github.com/Kyonax/org2html",
    "programmingLanguage": "TypeScript"
  }
}
#+END_JSONLD

A dynamic block, opened with =#+BEGIN:= and a name, holds whatever Emacs last
generated into it. This one is a column view of the tasks on this page, and its
captured table renders like any other:

#+BEGIN: columnview :hlines 1 :id global :format "%ITEM(Task) %TODO(State) %PRIORITY(Priority)"
| Task                          | State   | Priority |
|-------------------------------+---------+----------|
| Ship this reference post      | NEXT    | A        |
| Pick the slug and the date    | DONE    |          |
| Review the Spanish twin       | WAITING | 1        |
| Replace the placeholder cover | TODO    |          |
#+END:

=#+BEGIN_TABS= shows several alternatives in one place. Each =#+TAB:= line opens
a panel that can hold any block. With scripting off, every panel shows, one
after another:

#+BEGIN_TABS
#+TAB: Quote
#+BEGIN_QUOTE
A tab can hold any block the engine renders, not only a paragraph.
#+END_QUOTE
#+TAB: Example
#+BEGIN_EXAMPLE
$ org2html build content -o dist/blog
#+END_EXAMPLE
#+TAB: Table
| Panel   | Holds            |
|---------+------------------|
| Quote   | a quote block    |
| Example | an example block |
| Table   | this table       |
#+END_TABS

* Figures and media

An image link alone on its line, with a =#+CAPTION=, becomes a figure.
=#+NAME= gives it an anchor, so [[fig-main-figure][the main figure]] can be
linked by name, and =#+ATTR_O2H: :main t= marks it as the image that stands
for the whole page.

#+CAPTION: A captioned figure, named and marked as the page's main image.
#+NAME: fig-main-figure
#+ATTR_O2H: :main t
[[/blog/media/from-org-to-ast.png][Placeholder cover for From Org to AST]]

Without a caption it is still a figure, just an unlabelled one:

[[/blog/media/build-time-math.png][Placeholder cover for Mathematics at Build Time]]

An image inside a sentence, like this tiny gradient
[[/blog/media/sample.png][a tiny colour gradient]], stays inline.

=org-wide= breaks a figure out of the reading column, and =org-full-bleed= runs
it to both edges of the window:

#+CAPTION: A wide figure.
#+ATTR_HTML: :class org-wide
[[/blog/media/privacy-embeds.png][Placeholder cover for Embeds That Respect the Reader]]

#+CAPTION: A full-bleed figure.
#+ATTR_HTML: :class org-full-bleed
[[/blog/media/shipping-static.png][Placeholder cover for Shipping a Static Site That Stays Fast]]

=org-figure--bracket= and =org-figure--hatch= add the Style Book's two figure
decorations:

#+CAPTION: A bracketed figure.
#+ATTR_HTML: :class org-figure--bracket
[[/blog/media/a-style-book.png][Placeholder cover for A Style Book, Not a Framework]]

The remaining media arrive through =#+BEGIN_EXPORT html= blocks, and every one
of them passes through the sanitizer first. A row of images inside
=.org-carousel-strip= is a carousel that scrolls and snaps with CSS alone; the
runtime adds buttons and dots when scripting is on:

#+BEGIN_EXPORT html
<div class="org-carousel-strip">
  <img src="/blog/media/from-org-to-ast.png" alt="Placeholder cover for From Org to AST"
       width="1280" height="720" loading="lazy" decoding="async">
  <img src="/blog/media/privacy-embeds.png" alt="Placeholder cover for Embeds That Respect the Reader"
       width="1280" height="720" loading="lazy" decoding="async">
  <img src="/blog/media/shipping-static.png" alt="Placeholder cover for Shipping a Static Site That Stays Fast"
       width="1280" height="720" loading="lazy" decoding="async">
</div>
#+END_EXPORT

A diagram is authored SVG that carries classes and no colours of its own, so it
follows the Style Book. It is drawn 720 units wide and never shrinks below
700 pixels; on a narrow screen the frame scrolls instead, and with scripting on
it becomes a stage you can drag and zoom:

#+BEGIN_EXPORT html
<figure class="org-diagram">
<div class="org-diagram-scroll">
<svg class="org-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 720 200" role="img" aria-label="The org2html pipeline, from Org source to sanitized HTML">
<title>The org2html pipeline</title>
<defs>
<marker id="kitchen-sink-arrow" viewBox="0 0 8 8" refX="7" refY="4" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto">
<path class="org-diagram-arrow" d="M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 Z"/>
</marker>
</defs>
<text class="org-diagram-lane" x="24" y="30">AT BUILD TIME</text>
<rect class="org-diagram-band" x="12" y="44" width="696" height="112"/>
<g class="org-diagram-node"><rect x="24" y="72" width="104" height="56"/><text class="org-diagram-label" x="76" y="97" text-anchor="middle">RESOLVE</text><text class="org-diagram-sub" x="76" y="113" text-anchor="middle">includes</text></g>
<g class="org-diagram-node"><rect x="160" y="72" width="104" height="56"/><text class="org-diagram-label" x="212" y="97" text-anchor="middle">TOKENIZE</text><text class="org-diagram-sub" x="212" y="113" text-anchor="middle">lines</text></g>

#+END_EXPORT

A =<video>= keeps its native controls in the served page, so it plays with
scripting off, and the runtime then swaps in the Style Book's own controls; an
=<audio>= keeps the browser's. ~preload="none"~ means nothing is fetched until
you press play. The clip and the sound are CC0 samples from MDN's shared assets.

#+BEGIN_EXPORT html
<video controls preload="none" width="960" height="540" poster="/blog/media/everything-org2html-renders.png">
  <source src="https://mdn.github.io/shared-assets/videos/flower.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  A five-second clip of a flower opening.
</video>
#+END_EXPORT

#+BEGIN_EXPORT html
<audio controls preload="none">
  <source src="https://mdn.github.io/shared-assets/audio/t-rex-roar.mp3" type="audio/mpeg">
  A short roar, as an audio sample.
</audio>
#+END_EXPORT

Plain HTML survives too, as long as the sanitizer considers it safe: a
disclosure, a keyboard key and an abbreviation.

#+BEGIN_EXPORT html
<details>
  <summary>How do I export this file from Emacs?</summary>
  <p>Press <kbd>C-c</kbd> <kbd>C-e</kbd> to open the export dispatcher. This
  site never does: it builds from the command line with the
  <abbr title="Org-to-HTML converter">org2html</abbr> CLI.</p>
</details>
#+END_EXPORT

* Embeds

An embed is a facade. The page carries a poster and a play target, and the
provider's player loads only after a click, so a reader who never presses play
never talks to the provider. The same video three ways: in the column, wide,
and full-bleed with its channel named on the source line.

{{< youtube id="jNQXAC9IVRw" title="Me at the zoo" >}}

{{< youtube id="jNQXAC9IVRw" title="Me at the zoo, wide" wide="t" >}}

{{< youtube id="jNQXAC9IVRw" title="Me at the zoo, full-bleed" bleed="t" channel="jawed" >}}

A post from X works on the same terms. X publishes no poster, so =poster= names
a local image; =video= names the media file, which a click mounts as a real
=<video>= instead of a frame; =handle= names the account on the source line.

{{< x src="https://x.com/kyonax_on_tech/status/2094691954227400762/video/1" title="A post from the engine's author" poster="/blog/media/privacy-embeds.png" video="https://video.twimg.com/x.mp4" handle="kyonax_on_tech" >}}

A component is an inert placeholder a host can hydrate. Inside a sentence it
stays a =<span>=, like this badge {{< badge count="3" >}}, so the paragraph is
not split. As a block it can take its props as a JSON body:

#+BEGIN_COMPONENT card :title Reference card :variant compact
{"sections": ["headings", "tables", "math"]}
#+END_COMPONENT

* Inline

** Emphasis and code

Six markers: *bold*, /italic/, _underlined_, +struck through+, ~code~ and
=verbatim=. They nest, as in */bold italic/* and _/underlined italic/_.
Code and verbatim take their contents literally, however long:
~tokenizeParseRenderSanitizeAndShipEveryOrgConstructToStaticHtmlAtBuild~ and
=KITCHEN_SINK_EVERY_CONSTRUCT_THE_ENGINE_PARSES_RENDERS_WITHOUT_RUNTIME= are
seventy characters each.

** Sub- and superscripts and entities

With =^:{}=, braces are required: H_{2}O and E = mc^{2} render as sub- and
superscripts, while snake_case_names and 2^10 stay exactly as typed.

Entities spell a glyph by name, so =\alpha= renders as \alpha. This sentence
carries twelve of them: \alpha, \beta and \pi; \to, \times and \pm; \le, \ge
and \infty; 21\deg{}C; a literal \vert{} pipe; and a non-breaking space in
5\nbsp{}km.

** Citations, targets and fuzzy links

A citation keeps its key in a marked span for a host to resolve:
[cite:@dominik2010], or several at once, [cite/t:@dominik2010;@schulte2012].

A dedicated target marks a spot: <<the dedicated target>>this sentence carries
one. A radio target marks a spot the same way, <<<radio target>>> and a link
can jump to either.

A link with no scheme is fuzzy. It finds a target, as in
[[the dedicated target][back to the target]] and
[[radio target][to the radio target]]; a headline, as in
[[Math][the math section]]; or a =#+NAME=, as in
[[fig-main-figure][the main figure]]. A star forces a headline, as in
[[*Tables][the tables]], and a hash forces a =CUSTOM_ID=, as in
[[#every-link-scheme][the list of link schemes]].

** Every link scheme
:PROPERTIES:
:CUSTOM_ID: every-link-scheme
:END:

A described link, [[https://orgmode.org/manual/Hyperlinks.html][the Org manual
on hyperlinks]], and a bare URL of 120 characters, a permalink to the lines of
the engine that turn hyphens into dashes and curl straight quotes:
https://github.com/Kyonax/org2html/blob/8c19b203b8180ab03c97461122c531d4dae83b88/src/renderer/html-renderer.ts#L533-L552

An angle-bracketed link, <https://orgmode.org/manual/External-Links.html>; an
email address, [[mailto:hello@example.com][hello@example.com]]; a phone number,
[[tel:+15555550123][+1 555 555 0123]]; and an FTP server,
[[ftp://ftp.gnu.org/gnu/emacs/][the GNU Emacs archive]].

A =file:= link becomes a path on this site, as with [[file:/blog/o2h.js][the
runtime script this page loads]]. =id:= and =roam:= links point into an Emacs
knowledge base that does not exist on the web, so the engine renders them as
links to nowhere, =#=, by design: [[id:5b0e3f5c-2d6a-4b8e-9a51-7f2c8d0e1a34][an
id link]] and [[roam:Org syntax][a roam link]].

=#+LINK: engine …= defines an abbreviation, so [[engine:src/parser/parser.ts][the
parser]] expands to the full address of the engine's parser source.

** Timestamps

An active stamp, <2026-08-13 Thu>; an inactive one, [2026-08-13 Thu]; one with
a time, <2026-08-13 Thu 09:30>; a time range, <2026-08-13 Thu 09:30-11:00>; a
date range, <2026-08-13 Thu>--<2026-08-15 Sat>; and a repeater,
<2026-08-17 Mon +1w>. Each keeps its text and gains a =datetime=.

** Macros, link abbreviations and export snippets

=#+MACRO:= defines a template with numbered arguments. This page defines two:
{{{kbd(C-c C-e)}}} takes one argument and {{{keys(C-c C-e,h h)}}} takes two.
Built-in macros read the document itself: this is {{{title}}}, by {{{author}}},
dated {{{date}}}, filed under {{{keyword(CATEGORY)}}}, with the translation key
{{{property(TRANSLATION_KEY)}}}. =#+SETUPFILE= brings in the macros every post
on this blog shares, which is how {{{sitename}}} got into the first paragraph.

An export snippet speaks to one backend only: @@html:<mark>this mark reached the
page</mark>@@, and a LaTeX snippet right here @@latex:\newpage@@ was dropped.

* Math

Mathematics is typeset to MathML while the site builds, so the page ships no
typesetter. Inline, with dollars, $E = mc^2$, or with parentheses,
\(a^2 + b^2 = c^2\). On its own line, with double dollars:

$$\sum_{i=1}^{n} i = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$$

With square brackets:

\[ \int_0^1 x^2 \, dx = \frac{1}{3} \]

As a numbered equation:

\begin{equation}
e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0
\end{equation}

As an aligned derivation, with a second line wider than sixty characters:

\begin{align*}
(x + 1)^2 &= x^2 + 2x + 1 \\
          &= \sum_{k=0}^{2} \binom{2}{k} x^k + \int_0^x 0 \, dt - \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n}
\end{align*}

And a matrix:

\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 \\
0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}

A dollar sign is not always mathematics: this costs $5 and that costs $10, and
neither amount became a formula.

* Footnotes

A numbered footnote[fn:1], a named one[fn:setup], one defined inline where it
is used[fn:inline: An inline definition lives inside the reference itself.],
and an anonymous one[fn:: No label at all, and the engine numbers it anyway.].
Every kind lands in the same numbered list at the end of the page.

[fn:1] A numbered footnote. Its body can carry a long link, such as the lines
of the parser that read footnote references like these:
https://github.com/Kyonax/org2html/blob/8c19b203b8180ab03c97461122c531d4dae83b88/src/parser/parser.ts#L1606-L1629

[fn:setup] A named footnote, labelled =setup= in the source. Named and numbered
footnotes share one sequence.

* Includes

=#+INCLUDE:= splices another file into the page before anything is parsed. The
engine reads only from the document's own folder and from folders the build
names with =--include-root=, so a stray path cannot publish a file nobody
offered. These lines produced the rest of this section:

#+BEGIN_EXAMPLE
,#+INCLUDE: "../../includes/snippet.org"
,#+INCLUDE: "../../includes/sample.js" src js
,#+INCLUDE: "../../includes/setup.org" example
,#+INCLUDE: "../../includes/kitchen-sink-lexer.js" src javascript :lines "3-9"
,#+INCLUDE: "../../includes/kitchen-sink.en.org::*Only the body arrives" :only-contents t
,#+INCLUDE: "../../includes/kitchen-sink.en.org::*A part shifted down a level" :minlevel 2
#+END_EXAMPLE

A plain include brings in Org prose, parsed as if it had been typed here:

#+INCLUDE: "../../includes/snippet.org"

=src js= wraps the file in a source block, highlighted like any other:

#+INCLUDE: "../../includes/sample.js" src js

=example= wraps it in an example block instead. This is the setup file every
post on this blog pulls in; this page's own =#+OPTIONS= line wins over the one
inside it:

#+INCLUDE: "../../includes/setup.org" example

=:lines "3-9"= takes a slice of the file, so the comments above the function
and the export below it stay behind:

#+INCLUDE: "../../includes/kitchen-sink-lexer.js" src javascript :lines "3-9"

=::*Headline= picks one subtree by its title, and =:only-contents t= drops the
headline itself, so only its body arrives:

#+INCLUDE: "../../includes/kitchen-sink.en.org::*Only the body arrives" :only-contents t

=:minlevel 2= shifts a subtree's headlines until the shallowest sits at level
two, which files it under this section instead of starting a new one:

#+INCLUDE: "../../includes/kitchen-sink.en.org::*A part shifted down a level" :minlevel 2

* Reading the source

Every construct above came from one plain-text file and a handful of small
includes, rendered by the same build as every other post here. Open the source
beside this page and each family lines up with its section.
